title: Wood Mackenzie: European Gas Storage at risk of being below 70% ahead of Winter 2026/27
gist: Wood Mackenzie warns that near-record-low European gas storage combined with a renewed Strait of Hormuz disruption has pushed spot prices up more than 50% since June, and even a best-case Qatari supply recovery leaves Europe entering winter 2026/27 at only 75% storage versus a 90% five-year average.

insights.claim: European gas storage stood at just above 50% (54% per Wood Mackenzie's key findings) in late July 2026, a historically low level for that time of year.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Track weekly EU gas storage fill data as a near-term leading indicator for winter 2026/27 price spikes.
insights.quote: Storage across Europe stands at just above 50%, a historically low level for late July.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie's analysis warns that European gas storage

insights.claim: Even in Wood Mackenzie's best-case scenario, where Qatar reaches full operational LNG capacity (excluding damaged trains) by end of September 2026, European gas storage would only reach 75% by 1 November 2026, well below the 90% five-year average for that date.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 15-point storage shortfall versus the historical average implies structurally tighter winter gas balances and elevated price floors even under favorable assumptions.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie's analysis suggests European storage reaches 75% at best by 1 November. The five-year average for that date is 90%.

insights.claim: If the Strait of Hormuz remains closed for a further two months beyond Wood Mackenzie's base assumptions, European storage would end up below 70%, pushing prices higher and triggering demand destruction in some emerging Asian economies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A prolonged Strait of Hormuz closure is a distinct downside tail risk investors should monitor as a trigger for a second leg up in gas and LNG prices.
insights.quote: Should the Strait remain closed for a further two months, storage will end up lower than 70%.

insights.claim: European gas spot prices are up more than 50% since their 12 June 2026 lows and are trading above €60/MWh (US$20/mmbtu), with gas proving more sensitive to the Strait of Hormuz disruption than oil.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The outsized gas-versus-oil price reaction to the same geopolitical shock signals gas market tightness is the dominant driver, not just a generic risk-off move in energy.
insights.quote: Spot prices are up more than 50% since 12 June and trading above €60/MWh (US$20/mmbtu). Gas is proving more sensitive than oil to the disruption.

insights.claim: Unlike the 2022 crisis following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, current European gas prices have not returned to those record highs, partly because sustained investment in European renewables capacity since 2022 has reduced the power sector's exposure to gas prices — but Wood Mackenzie says Europe is nonetheless approaching energy crisis territory with limited near-term alternatives to gas.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Renewables buildout has structurally lowered Europe's gas-price sensitivity versus 2022, which caps (but does not eliminate) upside price risk this winter — relevant for utilities and power-price forecasting.
insights.quote: This is not 2022. Prices have not returned to the records set after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine removed major pipeline supply, and sustained investment in European renewables capacity since then has reduced power market exposure.

insights.claim: Asian LNG demand has returned to 2025 levels despite a continuing shortfall in Qatari export volumes, intensifying competition with Europe for available LNG cargoes.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rebounding Asian demand removes a key slack variable Europe has historically relied on to absorb LNG cargoes during supply disruptions.
insights.quote: Asian LNG demand has returned to 2025 levels, despite the shortfall in Qatari volumes, sharpening competition with Europe for available cargoes.
insights.locator: Three pressures are bearing down at once

insights.claim: No significant new LNG supply growth is expected globally over the next 9 to 12 months, with Qatari developments not expected to return to full capacity before the second half of 2027.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A near-term LNG supply wall through mid-2027 argues for elevated price floors persisting well beyond this winter, not just a transient spike.
insights.quote: No significant new LNG supply is expected over the next 9 to 12 months, with new Qatari capacity not online before the second half of 2027.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie now expects the global LNG market to rebalance only from 2028, as sustained disruption or new geopolitical risks reduce both the duration and depth of the previously anticipated global LNG oversupply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A pushed-back LNG oversupply timeline (to 2028) is a material revision for anyone positioned for a 2026/2027 LNG glut and falling prices.
insights.quote: LNG market might only rebalance from 2028. Sustained disruption or new geopolitical risks is poised to reduce both the duration and the depth of the anticipated global LNG oversupply.

insights.claim: High LNG costs are already straining some emerging Asian economies, which face outright demand destruction rather than just price pain, whereas wealthier nations can absorb the higher cost.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch lower-income Asian LNG importers for demand-destruction signals (curtailed industrial gas use, fuel switching) as an early indicator of how tight the global LNG market truly is.
insights.quote: Some emerging Asian economies face demand destruction, not just price pain. Wealthier nations can absorb the cost. Lower-income markets cannot.

insights.claim: The EU faces a difficult trade-off: its proposed ban on all Russian LNG imports starting January 2027, combined with more stringent methane emission regulations, could constrain import flexibility at precisely the moment Europe needs maximum flexibility to secure winter gas supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: EU policymakers may face pressure to delay or soften the Russian LNG import ban or methane rules if the supply crunch worsens — a policy risk worth tracking for gas and LNG traders.
insights.quote: the EU faces a difficult calculation: pressing ahead with both a proposed ban on all Russian LNG imports from January 2027 and more stringent methane emission regulations could constrain import flexibility at precisely the moment Europe needs it most.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Vice President of Gas and LNG Research, Massimo Di Odoardo, says the combination of low European inventories, strong Asian demand and limited new LNG supply growth almost guarantees elevated gas prices through winter 2026/27 and into 2027.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A named senior analyst's high-conviction call for sustained elevated prices through 2027, not just a single winter, is a signal to extend hedging/positioning horizons beyond the immediate season.
insights.quote: Low European inventories, strong Asian demand and limited new LNG supply growth almost guarantee elevated prices through this winter and into 2027

insights.claim: The global gas industry will convene at the Gastech 2026 conference in Bangkok in September 2026, where supply resilience is expected to define the agenda.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gastech 2026 in Bangkok (September) is a near-term event to watch for industry commentary, deals, or policy signals on LNG supply resilience.
insights.quote: The global gas industry convenes at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok in September. Supply resilience will define the agenda.
